Financial Inclusion and Credit Impacts on Crop Production in Ghana

Mark Appiah-Twumasi; Francis Tsiboe; Aisha Adam; Sylvanus Gaku; Peter Quartey

Abstract

Keywords: financial inclusion; credit; mobile money; technical efficiency; meta-stochastic frontier; Ghana

JEL Classification: G21, G51, O13, Q12, Q14

1. Introduction

Financial inclusion, defined as improved access to savings, credit, digital payments, and insurance, is central to the development strategy of agro-based economies in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) such as Ghana (Demirguc-Kunt et al., 2017; Ogundari, 2014). In Ghana, recent reports document an expansion in access to (in)formal financial services over the past decade, and mobile money platforms have extended outreach into remote areas (Ghana Statistical Service (GSS), 2019, 2014; Klapper et al., 2025). In theory, relaxing liquidity constraints should foster poverty reduction and food security by enabling farmers to undertake lumpy, yield-enhancing investments (e.g., fertilizer, improved seeds, mechanization) and thereby operate nearer to best-practice production frontiers. In practice, however, the evidence for Ghana is mixed across settings and services.

Studies on credit and farm performance in Ghana often focus on specific crops or regions and rely on cross-sectional data. For instance, participation in input credit schemes in Northern Ghana increased use of fertilizer and labor but yielded only modest output gains and no significant income effects among maize farmers (Iddrisu et al., 2018). Similarly, among smallholder rice producers, access to bank‐linked credit did not raise technical efficiency relative to non‐borrowers (Anang et al., 2016). By contrast, work on maize shows that both formal and informal financing are associated with improved technical and/or economic efficiency (Appiah-Twumasi et al., 2022; Martey et al., 2019). Recent evidence on starchy staples suggests that pure technical inefficiency, rather than technology gaps, explains a larger share of production shortfalls across ecologies (Ansah et al., 2023a). Collectively, these results sharpen a clear research gap which this study addresses: does expanded financial inclusion—operationalized here as access to and use of credit—move Ghanaian farms toward the best-practice frontier, or does it mainly raise input intensity without proportional efficiency gains?

To address this question, we merge nationally representative microdata from waves 6 (2012/13) and 7 (2016/17) of the Ghana Living Standards Survey (GLSS), with a stochastic metafrontier (SMF) framework and nearest neighbor matching (NNM). This period brackets comparable agricultural/finance modules and coincides with the rapid diffusion of digital finance in Ghana, allowing us to study credit effects under meaningful institutional change (Ghana Statistical Service (GSS), 2019, 2014; World Bank, 2024). Our approach estimates how credit access affects farmers’ input elasticities (responsiveness of output to land, seed, labor, and agrochemicals) while separately quantifying shifts in pure technical efficiency (TE), the technology gap ratio [TGR] (distance to best‐practice frontiers), and meta‐frontier technical efficiency (MTE), under heterogeneous technologies. Viewing NNM as addressing selection on observables; we investigate robustness via alternative specifications and interpret the results accordingly.

Credit use makes a practical difference in how farmers run a season. With a loan in hand, they can buy improved seeds before prices jump, pay for fertilizer and pesticides when crops need them, and hire extra hands for land prep, weeding, and harvest. Many also adopt practices used by the best performers—like timely spraying, better spacing, or renting a sheller for post-harvest. In our data, borrowers look more like these “best-practice” farms, meaning credit helps pull them toward better technology and timing. But getting closer isn’t the same as getting there. Some borrowers still face a learning curve using new inputs, struggle with delayed deliveries, or stretch loans across too many needs. Those frictions show up as lower day-to-day efficiency even when the toolkit is better.

That’s why the policy message isn’t just “more credit,” it’s better credit. Loans need to arrive before planting, be sized to the crop, and repay after harvest; simple digital disbursement helps but so do guarantees that inputs are genuine and arrive on time. Bundling finance with practical extension (what to do, when, and how), basic record-keeping tools, soil testing, and links to buyers can turn borrowed cedis into reliable yield gains. For riskier seasons, pairing credit with weather insurance or flexible grace periods keeps farmers from backsliding. In short: when credit is matched with the right advice, inputs, and timing, farmers don’t just spend more—they farm smarter.

We advance the literature in three ways. First, we go beyond single-crop and single-region analyses by providing nationally representative evidence that jointly characterizes movement toward the frontier (TGR) and movement along it (TE) under credit access. Second, by using an SMF, we ensure comparability of estimates across heterogeneous technologies driven by a producers financial inclusion status, a critical improvement over studies that assume a common production technology (e.g., Abdul-Rahaman et al., 2021; Appiah-Twumasi et al., 2022). Third, we document systematic heterogeneity by gender, crop, and agro-ecological zone, clarifying where and for whom financial inclusion is most likely to generate productivity-enhancing effects rather than efficiency losses (Anang et al., 2016; Martey et al., 2019).

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the data and summarizes key descriptive statistics. Section 3 examines the evolving financial service environment among crop producers. Section 4 outlines the meta‐stochastic frontier and matching methodology. Section 5 presents empirical results and discussion. Finally, Section 6 concludes with policy implications and directions for future research.

2. Data sources and sample description

We use farm-level microdata from the Ghana Living Standards Survey (GLSS) Waves 6 (2012/13) and 7 (2016/17). Both waves are repeated cross-sections drawn via a two-stage design (enumeration areas, then households). Following the GLSS documentation, (Tsiboe, 2020) consolidate the raw files to a farmer-level dataset that has supported several analyses of agricultural productivity in Ghana [21], [22], [23], [25], [26]. Our study focuses on crop farmers, trimming yield outliers by keeping observations with yields (kg/ha) between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles within survey round × crop. As shown in Table 1, the final sample comprises 15,860 farm operators cultivating at least one of the following: banana, beans, cashew, cassava, citrus, cocoa, coconut, cocoyam, cotton/kenaf, maize, millet, oil-palm, groundnut, plantain, potato, rice, sorghum, yam, sugarcane, tomato, pepper, okra, onion, eggplant, and other minor crops.

The consolidated files do not include a pre-built financial-inclusion module, so we reconstruct credit and financial-service indicators directly from the original GLSS questionnaires. Using preserved enumeration-area, household, and member IDs, we extract items from Section 12 (credit, assets, savings, and use of financial services; see Exhibits S1–S2) and merge them to the farmer-level file. Tables 2–3 summarize the specific variables (with questionnaire item numbers). We define credit use at the individual level as having an approved loan application or a positive amount borrowed in the past 12 months. Our preferred treatment is a household-level indicator equal to 1 if the farmer, spouse/children, or another household member meets this criterion (capturing intra-household pooling). By this definition, 8.86%% of sample households used credit; component shares are 6.30%% farmer, 3.18%% spouse, and 6.63%% other member—not mutually exclusive, hence their sum exceeds 8.86%%. Unless stated otherwise, “credit user(s)” refers to this household-level measure; a farmer-only variant is used in robustness checks.

Table 1 reports descriptive statistics of the pooled and credit-disaggregated samples, focusing on farmer, crop, and household characteristics. Female farmers account for 25% of the pooled sample and the average farmer is 47.28 years old with a little over 4.31 years of schooling. Mean household size is about 5.52 adult equivalents (AE) and the dependency ratio 1.43. Consistent with national statistics on smallholder farmers (Ministry of Food and Agriculture (MoFA), 2017), farms in our sample averages less than 2 ha (≈1.84 ha), of which 63% is owned, and crop diversification score is 0.47 on our index.

Comparatively, credit users do not differ by household size or dependency ratios from non-users, but they are significantly younger (45.77 vs. 47.43 years) and more educated (6.12 vs. 4.14 years). Baseline per-hectare yields are statistically similar at 5% level for all crops except rice and yam (where non-users edge out users) and cocoyam and tomato (users outperform non-users). Additionally, credit access appears to be associated with increased hired labor employment and pesticide use, but not with other inputs. Moreover, over 2012–2017 fertilizer use among credit users increased by 16.29 kg/ha annually, while it remained statistically flat for non-users. Together, these statistics suggest largely uniform balance (and therefore, comparability) between users and non-users. Notwithstanding, the isolated imbalances between treated and control households justify our use of propensity score matching.

3. The state of financial inclusion and credit access

To contextualize the credit access landscape in Ghana, we examine indicators (Tables 2 and 3) of account ownership, participation in financial schemes, self-reported barriers, institutional channels, products, outreach, infrastructure, insurance enrollment, and loan application outcomes. A composite financial inclusion score (Table 2, last row) summarizes these dimensions, while Table 3 presents farmers’ loan application outcomes across the two survey waves.

3.1 Account Ownership and Barriers to Participation

Account ownership remains a core marker of financial inclusion. Globally, the share of adults with an account rose from 51 percent in 2011 to 69 percent in 2017. Among Ghanaian crop farmers, the increase was slower but still notable: formal account ownership grew from roughly one-quarter in 2012/13 to over one-third in 2016/17. This rise is mirrored in the composite financial inclusion index, though at its peak only 36.2% of households engaged in banks or savings schemes, leaving a large share unbanked. The main self-reported barrier is lack of funds, with nearly 60.4% of non-account holders citing “not enough money,” a figure that edged upward between waves and aligns with global evidence on income volatility as the chief exclusion driver (Klapper et al., 2025). A smaller but growing share reported “no need for an account,” suggesting reliance on informal channels or mistrust of formal services. Distance to institutions declined in importance, reflecting infrastructure improvements, while paperwork burdens and awareness gaps persisted at low but steady levels.

3.2 Channels, Products, and Digital Services

Institutional channels have shifted markedly. Traditional banks—commercial, community, and rural—still serve the majority but fell from nearly 68.1% to about half of account holders between the two survey waves. Mobile money platforms emerged rapidly, reaching over one-third of users by 2016/17 (Aker and Mbiti, 2010), while informal susu schemes and savings groups remained stable around 16.1%. Product uptake is dominated by savings accounts; current, investment, and other more sophisticated products remain rare. Use of transaction services is limited: ATM cards and e-banking penetration remain below 3.2%, while cheque usage nearly doubled but from a very low base. These gaps reflect constraints in rural electricity and internet infrastructure but also highlight the untapped potential of digital services for streamlining farm transactions and record-keeping.

3.3 Outreach, Information, and Insurance

Sources of financial information have also shifted. Personal networks have grown in importance, with colleagues and relatives informing over half of account holders in 2016/17, up from 39.0%, while radio’s role halved. This suggests that peer effects and trusted networks are more effective than mass media in promoting financial products among rural farmers. Infrastructure improvements reinforced these changes: average distance to the nearest bank fell by roughly five kilometers, and proximity to roads and transport also improved. On the risk-management side, health insurance enrollment rose appreciably due to public campaigns, but uptake of life, pension, and agricultural insurance remained negligible. Yet studies show strong farmers’ willingness to adopt index-based agricultural insurance under the right conditions (Ali et al., 2020; Oppong Mensah et al., 2023), pointing to a gap between latent demand and product availability.

3.4 Loan Applications and Credit Use

Credit application rates remain low: only about 9.8% of farmers applied for a loan in either wave, with application rates essentially flat. Approval rates, however, improved, with two-thirds of applicants obtaining credit and rejection rates halving—possibly reflecting either more accommodating lenders or better borrower–lender matching. Still, average loan sizes declined, and sources shifted: group-based microfinance rose from 23.8% to nearly 39.2% of loans, while reliance on friends and formal banks declined (Appiah-Twumasi et al., 2019; Karlan et al., 2017). Notably, the share of loans used explicitly for agricultural purposes dropped sharply, suggesting growing nonfarm diversification, lender restrictions, or diversion of agricultural loans (Hussain and Thapa, 2016). Collateral requirements eased as unsecured lending grew from two-thirds to more than three-quarters of cases, yet lack of collateral remained the leading reason for rejection. More than half of non-applicants cited “no need for a loan,” even as physical and institutional constraints diminished. This points to a persistent demand-side bottleneck: expanding credit supply alone may not be sufficient unless products are better aligned with farmers’ production needs and perceptions of value (De Janvry and Sadoulet, 2020).

4. Empirical methods

Guided by Ghanaian and broader SSA literature, we posit the following hypotheses. H1 (Frontier adoption): credit access increases TGR by easing liquidity constraints for lumpy, technology-enhancing investments. H2 (Efficiency trade-off): without complementary agronomic knowledge, risk-management, and timely input delivery, credit-enabled adoption may reduce TE via misallocation, learning frictions, or risk-induced input timing errors. H3 (Input intensification): credit raises responsiveness to land and labor relative to fertilizer, reflecting managerial and timing constraints in input quality and application. These hypotheses will be tested within the SMF-PSM framework using GLSS 6–7. The above hypotheses have direct relevance for national agricultural policy formulation. If credit systematically narrows technology gaps but depresses efficiency, then bundled interventions e.g., pairing credit with extension, appropriate risk instruments, and increased payment delivery networks, are required to convert access into sustained productivity gains in Ghana’s smallholder sector (Barrett et al., 2022; Meyer, 2015; World Bank, 2024).

4.1 Meta-stochastic frontier analysis

Rising access to basic financial services amid shallow usage suggests that credit users and non-users face different financing constraints and, plausibly, different production technologies. Estimating a single common frontier would confound technology differences with managerial efficiency. We therefore model heterogeneous technologies for credit users and non-users and compare producers against a common stochastic metafrontier (SMF) to separate (i) proximity to best-practice technology (TGR) from (ii) within-technology technical efficiency (TE). The product of the two yields meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE).

We estimate separate stochastic production frontiers (SFs) for group \(j \in \{\text{credit user},\ \text{non-user}\}\) using a translog form for flexibility:

\[ f^{j}(x_{ijt}) = \ln(y_{ijt}) = \beta_{0r} + \sum_{k} \beta_{kj}\ln(x_{kijt}) + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}\sum_{k} \beta_{skj}\log\ln(x_{kijt})\ln(x_{sijt}) + \beta_{h}h_{ijt} + v_{ijt} - u_{ijt} \]

\[ u_{ijt} \sim N^{+}\!\left(0,\ \exp(w_{ijt}\alpha)\right),\qquad v_{ijt} \sim N\!\left(0,\ \sigma_{vj}^{2}\right) \qquad\qquad (1) \]

Here, \(y_{ijt}\) is crop output value for for the ith farmer in group j for survey t; inputs \(x_{kijt}\) include land, planting materials, both family and hired labor, fertilizer, and pesticide; vector \(h_{ijt}\) contains technology shifters and controls (crop-mix shares, survey wave, ecological zone). The composite error has two-sided noise \(\sigma_{v}^{2}\) [\(v_{ijt} \sim N(0, \sigma_{vj}^{2})\)] (Belotti et al., 2013) and one-sided inefficiency \(u_{ijt} \ge 0\). Following standard practice, we opted for a half-normal distribution for \(u_{ijt}\) (i.e., \(u_{ijt} \sim N^{+}(0, \exp(w_{ijt}\alpha_{j}))\)) having encountered issues with convergence for other distributions in the case of sub-sample estimations. However, alternative distributions (exponential, truncated-normal, gamma) were assessed and produced similar inferences. Determinants of inefficiency enter via a scaling function as \(\sigma_{u_{ijt}}^{2} = \exp(w_{ijt}\alpha_{j})\), where \(w_{ijt}\) includes covariates influencing technical inefficiency and \(\alpha\) represents a vector of parameters to be estimated. Following previous works (Adaku et al., 2023; Ansah et al., 2023b; Asravor et al., 2024; Tsiboe et al., 2021), \(w_{ijt}\) contained farmer characteristics (age, education, and gender), institutional factors (land ownership, credit, mechanization, and extension), crop diversification, fixed effects for ecological zone and GLSS waves, and a constant term.

Given the SF production function for the jth group, the “pure farmer technical efficiency” (TE) of the ith farmer is calculated as:

\[ TE_{ijt} = E\!\left(\exp(-u_{ijt}) \mid \varepsilon_{ijt}\right) \qquad\qquad (2) \]

To benchmark heterogeneous group frontiers against a common technology set, we estimate a stochastic metafrontier that envelops the group-specific SFs:

\[ f^{M}(x_{ijt}) = \ln(y_{ijt}) = \beta_{0r} + \sum_{k} \beta_{kM}\ln(x_{kiMt}) + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}\sum_{k} \beta_{skM}\log\ln(x_{kiMt})\ln(x_{siMt}) + \beta_{h}h_{ijt} - u_{Mijt} \qquad\qquad (3) \]

Where \(u_{iM} \sim N^{+}(0, \exp(w_{i}\alpha_{M}))\) is strictly positive, implying that \(f^{j}(x_{ijt}) \le f^{M}(x_{ijt})\). Consequently, the ratio of group j’s stochastic frontier to the MSF is the technology gap ratio (TGR), which is represented as:

\[ TGR_{ijt} = \frac{f^{j}(x_{ijt})}{f^{M}(x_{ijt})} = e^{-u_{iM}} \le 1 \qquad\qquad (4) \]

and meta-frontier technical efficiency decomposes as

\[ MTE_{ijt} = f^{j}(x_{ijt})\left(f^{M}(x_{ijt})\,e^{v_{ijt}}\right)^{-1} = TGR_{ijt} \times TE_{ijt} \qquad\qquad (5) \]

This decomposition separates movement toward the best-practice technology set (TGR) from movement along a group’s frontier (TE).

We implement a two-step SMF: (i) estimate group SFs in (1) by MLE, obtain TE; (ii) estimate the metafrontier in (4) on the pooled sample to recover TGR and hence MTE via (6). Input elasticities are the first derivatives of the estimated frontiers evaluated at sample means; returns to scale (RTS) equal the sum of elasticities. Regularity (monotonicity, curvature) is checked at means; the SMF envelopment improves shape-regularity relative to a pooled single frontier. “Credit status” defines the groups (users vs non-users) and is measured at the household level in the preferred specification; robustness to narrower definitions (farmer-only) is reported elsewhere.

4.2 Forming comparable pairs of farmers

Several features could bias estimates: self-reported credit use (recall/social-desirability error and misclassification), non-random credit access (lender targeting and farmer self-selection), and treatment definitions (household-level vs farmer-only). Matching addresses selection on observables but not all unobservables (e.g., ability, risk preferences, networks), so we report robustness to alternative definitions, algorithms, and production-function forms and interpret remaining bias conservatively.

We construct a matched sample to estimate the metafrontier in Equation (3). Each credit user is paired one-to-one with a non-user of similar characteristics (Abadie and Imbens, 2016, 2006), creating balance for the pooled SMF while preserving the user/non-user technology split. Exact matching is enforced within operator gender, GLSS wave, region, agro-ecology, and rural/urban status. Additional covariates for distance calculation include farmer demographics (age, education, marital status, religion, ethnicity, relation to household head), household composition (size, dependency ratio, female share), production choices (crop diversification, land shares by crop), and tenure/land ownership. This design isolates technological differences associated with credit from compositional differences in who borrows.

To form pairs, we implement nearest-neighbor matching under multiple distance metrics—propensity scores (logit, probit, complementary log–log, cauchit), Euclidean/scaled-Euclidean, and (robust) Mahalanobis (Rosenbaum, 2020, 2010). Balance is assessed via standardized differences and variance ratios (targets ≈0 and ≈1, respectively) (Rubin, 2001; Stuart, 2010). As shown in Fig. S1, logit propensity-score distance delivers the best overall balance; nevertheless, the main results are stable across metrics. This matched-SMF approach follows prior MSF applications facing similar endogeneity concerns (Asmare et al., 2022; Bravo-Ureta et al., 2021; Crespo-Cebada et al., 2014; Mayen et al., 2010; Tiedemann and Latacz-Lohmann, 2013).

4.5 Estimating standard errors

We use a cluster jackknife at the Enumeration Area (EA) level. For each survey wave, we create 100 delete-one-EA replicates. In every replicate, one EA is removed, the remaining EAs from both waves are pooled, and the full pipeline is re-run: group frontiers are re-estimated with monotonicity and quasi-concavity regularization, matching is re-done, the metafrontier is re-estimated, and TE, TGR, MTE, and elasticities are re-computed. Jackknife standard errors are obtained from the dispersion of these replicate estimates, which captures uncertainty from clustering, matching, and frontier estimation in a unified way. We report two-sided tests and confidence intervals based on these jackknife standard errors, and results are similar when varying the number of replicates or using an EA-level bootstrap.

5. Results and discussion

We present diagnostics for the stochastic meta-frontier (SMF), input elasticities, technology differentials, robustness checks, and patterns of observed heterogeneity with particular emphasis on results from the matched sample.

5.1 Diagnostic test

Three sets of diagnostics support our use of the SMF and the half-normal inefficiency model. First, one-sided error tests (Coelli, 1995; Gutierrez et al., 2001; Schmidt and Lin, 1984) reported in Table 4 reject the null of no inefficiency across all model variants (naïve national frontier; group frontiers; meta-frontier on matched and unmatched samples).In addition, imposing envelopment restrictions and estimating a stochastic meta-frontier improves shape-regularity diagnostics relative to a pooled frontier: monotonicity and curvature satisfaction rates increase substantially in the matched sample, reducing concerns that elasticities reflect local violations of economic regularity. The monotonicity satisfaction rate rises to 100.00% and the curvature satisfaction rate to 84.00%% under the matched meta-frontier, compared to their respective analogues of 89.00% and 25.00%% in the unmatched meta-frontier and 47.00% and 21.00%% in the naïve specification (Table 4). Third, likelihood-ratio tests for the meta-frontier strongly favour the enveloping specification over a common frontier at 1% significance level in both the matched and unmatched models. Meanwhile, the share of variance attributable to inefficiency () is high under the meta-frontier (matched = 0.883; unmatched = 0.649), indicating that cross-household output differences are dominated by technology gaps rather than transitory noise. Collectively, these tests confirm that our estimation strategy is fit for purpose and that estimates are reliable.

5.2 Output elasticities

Table 4 compares national, group, and matched meta-frontier estimates of input elasticities. Under the naïve national frontier, all inputs exhibit positive and statistically significant effects on crop output at the 1% level, consistent with earlier Ghanaian studies (Akudugu et al., 2012; Enu et al., 2013; Karamba et al., 2011). Land exerts the strongest influence, followed by family labor, planting materials, fertilizer, hired labor, and pesticide.

The group frontier results show clear differences between borrowers and non-borrowers. Farmers with credit access display higher elasticities for nearly all inputs, with the largest gains observed for family labor (+0.064 percentage points) and land (+-0.001). Smaller but positive differences emerge for planting materials (+-0.003) and pesticide (+0.002) and hired labor (+-0.003). The only exception is fertilizer, where borrowers’ elasticity is slightly lower (0.015 vs. 0.014; –0.001). These shifts translate into higher returns to scale for borrowers (1.09 vs. 1.028), a statistically significant difference of +0.062.

These findings echo evidence from [insert countries], where credit programs facilitated more allocation and enabled greater responsiveness to variable production inputs [insert citations]. The fertilizer anomaly stands in contrast to Ethiopian studies showing that fertilizer adoption is constrained by risk/credit issues (Dercon and Christiaensen, 2011). However, it is consistent with research documenting Ghana’s persistently low and heterogeneous fertilizer returns, partly due to soil quality variation and input delivery inefficiencies [insert citations]. This suggests that credit alone may not raise fertilizer effectiveness unless complemented by agronomic support and input quality assurance.

The matched meta-frontier further reinforces these patterns. Elasticities at the mean are generally larger than in the unmatched specification, especially for inputs that are most marginally adjusted. Land responsiveness rises from 0.761 to 0.75, family labor from 0.165 to 0.183, and hired labor from 0.019 to 0.018. Pesticide use shows a notable increase (0.027 vs. 0.024), while fertilizer responsiveness is modestly lower (0.015 vs. 0.018). Overall, these results suggest that access to credit enhances farmers’ capacity to intensify labor and protection-related inputs, while the small decline in fertilizer elasticity may reflect substitution effects or measurement limitations. Taken together, the evidence points to credit easing liquidity constraints in ways that strengthen input responsiveness along margins most sensitive to timely financial access. This interpretation resonates with broader evidence on how digital financial innovations expand smallholder access to working capital and improve timely input use across African settings [insert citations].

5.3 Technology differential and technical efficiency

Table 4 further decomposes performance into differences in technology (TGR), within-group technical efficiency (TE), and their combination into meta-frontier efficiency (MTE).

Starting with technology gaps, the matched estimates show that borrowers are significantly closer to the best practice technology set. The technology gap ratio (TGR) rises from 0.883 for non-users to 0.864 for borrowers, a gain of -1.9 percentage points. In practical terms, credit is associated with greater adoption of advanced technologies—such as improved seeds, fertilizer blends, or mechanized services (citations). To attain comparable output levels, credit-constrained farmers would need to raise their technological endowments by roughly 13%.

By contrast, pure technical efficiency (TE) is markedly lower for borrowers. In the matched sample, TE falls from 0.54 among non-borrowers to 0.609 among borrowers—a difference of 6.9 percentage points. This suggests that conditional on their respective group technologies, borrowers operate farther from their potential frontier. While this result contradicts recent evidence from Ghana and other African contexts, which generally finds that credit-constrained farmers underperform relative to their efficient frontier (Awotide et al., 2015; Dessie, 2015), it may reflect transitional inefficiencies. For instance, credit may enable adoption of new technologies that are not yet mastered, introduce moral hazard in input use, or lead to resource misallocation when complementary services (e.g., training, extension, or timely input delivery) are lacking (Tsiboe et al., 2016).

Combining these two forces, meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE) is modestly lower for borrowers (0.527 vs. 0.478), a statistically significant difference of 4.9 percentage points. Thus, while credit facilitates convergence toward better technologies (higher TGR), it is also associated with reduced efficiency in operating those technologies (lower TE), yielding a small net decline in overall performance against best practice.

Finally, it is notable that both borrowers and non-borrowers operate below 53% of the best-practice frontier. Similar findings from other African settings attribute such low efficiency to limited application of essential inputs and persistent process inefficiencies, particularly delayed access to credit and weak market support systems (Guirkinger and Boucher, 2008; Kumar et al., 2013). This underscores that while credit access improves technological proximity, broader systemic interventions are needed to ensure that farmers can fully exploit the potential of advanced technologies.

5.4 Robustness of main findings

We next evaluate the robustness of the core finding that credit is associated with higher TGR but lower TE among credit users, resulting in modestly lower MTE. These contrasts remain qualitatively unchanged and statistically significant across alternative treatment definitions, model specifications, and matching methods. Table 5 first examines the definition of treatment. In our preferred specification, credit is broadly defined to include access by the farmer, spouse, children, or other household members. Under this definition, borrowers exhibit a TGR of 0.864 versus 0.883 for non-users (+-1.9 percentage points), TE of 0.609 versus 0.54 (−6.9), and MTE of 0.527 versus 0.478 (−4.9). Narrowing the treatment to only the farmer’s personal credit reduces the magnitudes but preserves the direction of effects: TGR improves by 1.6 percentage points, TE declines by about 5.5 points, and MTE is lower by roughly 6.1 points. Definitions based on spousal or other household members’ credit show comparable patterns, underscoring that the efficiency gap persists regardless of how credit access is measured.

Turning to methodological checks, the findings remain consistent across distance metrics used in the matching algorithm (Mahalanobis, Euclidean) and across alternative propensity score models with probit, logit, complementary log–log, or cauchit links (Figure S1). In every case, borrowers continue to display significantly higher TGR and lower TE. Likelihood-ratio tests favor a translog production structure over Cobb–Douglas, though re-estimating with Cobb–Douglas preserves the same ordering of TGR, TE, and MTE across credit groups (Figure S1). Varying the distributional assumption for the one-sided error term (exponential, truncated normal, gamma) produces substantively similar inferences, supporting the use of the half-normal baseline.

Taken together, the robustness checks summarized in Table 5 and the supplementary figures and tables demonstrate that the main conclusions are not driven by treatment definition, model specification, or distributional assumptions. Across specifications, credit users consistently appear closer to the best-practice technology set (higher TGR) but operate less efficiently within that set (lower TE), producing slightly lower overall performance relative to the meta-frontier (MTE).

5.5 Observed heterogeneity

We also explore heterogeneity across borrower characteristics, crop systems, and regions, and relate these patterns to the main findings. Figure 3 and Table S2 indicate that the technology gains from credit are not uniform: increases in TGR are largest among male, better-educated, and prime-age farmers, with correspondingly smaller penalties in TE. This gradient is consistent with the covariate associations in Table S4, which show that education and access to extension services are linked to lower inefficiency. Trade-offs between TGR and TE also vary by crop system. Borrowers in cocoa- and root/tuber-dominated areas experience larger technological gains but also steeper efficiency reductions, whereas maize-, sorghum-, and millet-based systems show more muted trade-offs. Regional heterogeneity similarly reflects agro-ecological conditions and market access, suggesting that credit facilitates technology adoption most where the technology–environment match is favorable but does not automatically improve within-group efficiency.

Input trends over 2012–2017 provide context for these patterns. Figures 1 and 2, together with Table S2, document rising seed expenditure and greater labor use, with little evidence of increased mechanization or irrigation. Figure 1 shows that input and output gaps between credit users and non-users largely mirror these intensification dynamics. Figure 2 further illustrates that the productivity advantage of credit users is strongest at higher levels of the composite financial inclusion index, underscoring complementarities between credit, payment systems, and access to information. Taken together, the results highlight that the credit–efficiency relationship is mediated by farmer characteristics, crop systems, and local institutions, with credit yielding the greatest technology gains where enabling conditions are present

6. Conclusion

The paper acknowledges the importance of credit and how it impacts crop production albeit with differentiated effects. We therefore posed the question: does expanded financial inclusion move Ghanaian farms toward the best-practice frontier, or does it mainly raise input intensity without proportional efficiency gains? By addressing this knowledge gap in both theoretical and empirical literature, our study advances literature in three ways. First, the analysis extends beyond single-crop and single-region investigation by providing nationally representative evidence that jointly characterizes movement toward the frontier (TGR) and movement along it (TE) under credit access. Second, our use of an SMF ensures comparability of estimates across heterogeneous crops and regional technologies; certainly, an improvement over studies that assume a common production technology. Finally, we document systematic heterogeneity by gender, crop, and agro-ecological zone, clarifying where and for whom credit is most likely to generate productivity-enhancing effects rather than efficiency losses. The paper employs a novel hybrid approach, combining a Stochastic Metafrontier (SMF) framework with Propensity Score Matching (PSM) on a nationally representative data from Waves 6 and 7 of the Ghana Living Standards Survey (GLSS).

Our analysis reveals that all factor inputs—land, labor, seed, and agrochemicals have a positive and statistically significant (at the 1% level) relationship with total crop output, with land exhibiting the strongest influence. Crucially, credit access amplifies farmers’ responsiveness to these inputs. In our matched sample, borrowers show higher output elasticities than their unmatched counterparts.

Disaggregating the efficiency effects yields nuanced insights; while credit facilitates investment in superior technology, narrowing the technology gap between borrower groups, it does not automatically translate into better farm management. Contrary to some existing studies, we find that borrowers are less technically efficient than non-borrowers, operating farther from their group’s best-practice frontier. This suggests that credit, while boosting output through input intensification and technology adoption, may simultaneously introduce inefficiencies in how those inputs are managed.

Alarmingly, both borrowers and non-borrowers in our sample operate below 53% of their potential output in our matched sample, constrained by limited and untimely access to credit. This restriction curtails the optimal application of essential inputs (e.g., fertilizer, quality seeds, labor) and heightens vulnerability to shocks, ultimately compromising overall yield and productivity.

Our findings underscore an urgent need for targeted policy interventions. Efforts must extend beyond simply expanding credit availability to ensure it is timely, accessible, and coupled with complementary support such as extension services and training. This also includes improving financial literacy and farm management skills to enhance technical efficiency, ensuring that credit translates into sustainable productivity gains. Such measures are vital for boosting agricultural output, promoting sustainable development, and contributing to economic growth in Ghana, where agriculture remains a cornerstone of the economy.
